title: Not by Bread Alone: Remember the Wilderness
summary: Moses tells Israel to remember the forty years in the wilderness, where God humbled and tested them, fed them with manna, and kept their clothes from wearing out, to teach them that people live by every word from God's mouth. He describes the rich land ahead and warns that when they are full and wealthy they must not grow proud and say that their own strength made them rich. Forgetting God, he says, will lead to the same ruin as the nations before them.
story: Chapter 7 dealt with the danger of Canaan's gods; chapter 8 returns to the danger chapter 6 first named, the quiet threat of plenty. Moses sets two places side by side in memory, the wilderness Israel is leaving and the fertile land they are entering, and argues that the first was training for the second. The people standing before him were children or not yet born when the wilderness years began, and now they are about to enter a land where they will never need manna again. The chapter asks what will keep them humble when hunger no longer does. Israel's later history, from Solomon's wealth to the prophets' charges against the comfortable rich, shows how searching the question was.
historical:
The chapter looks back on events told in Exodus and Numbers: the manna that began in the Wilderness of Sin (Exodus 16), water from the rock (Exodus 17; Numbers 20), and the fiery serpents in the desert (Numbers 21). Those forty years are counted from the departure from Egypt to the arrival on the plains of Moab; for the debate over when the exodus happened and when Deuteronomy took its final form, see the note on Deuteronomy 5.

The description of the land in verses 7 to 9 fits the southern Levant well. Its water came from springs and seasonal streams rather than a great river like the Nile, and its staple crops were exactly those listed: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and honey (probably including date syrup as well as bees' honey). Jewish tradition calls these the seven species. The line about rocks of iron and hills of copper reflects the region's mineral wealth; copper was mined in antiquity in the Arabah, south of the Dead Sea, at sites such as Faynan and Timna, where copper was worked from very early times and on a large scale in the Iron Age.
cultural:
For an ancient farmer, bread was life itself, and the word for bread often stands for food in general. That is why the sentence in verse 3 lands with such force: "man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD." In a world where famine was a constant fear, Moses says that bread is not the deepest thing a person depends on. Manna, the flaky food that appeared each morning in the wilderness, could not be stored except on the day before the Sabbath; it taught daily dependence by its very nature.

The picture of a father disciplining his son (verse 5) also belongs to the ancient household, where training a son was a father's duty and a sign of love, not rejection. And verse 10, "When you eat and are satisfied, you are to bless the LORD your God," became in Jewish practice the basis of the grace said after meals, a practice that keeps the chapter's lesson at the family table.
literary: The chapter is framed as a sermon on memory, and its key verbs are remember and forget (verses 2, 11, 14, 18, 19). It is built in a mirror pattern. The opening call to obey (verse 1) matches the closing warning (verses 19 and 20). The wilderness remembered (verses 2 to 6) matches the wilderness remembered again (verses 14 to 16). At the center stand the good land and the command to bless God when full (verses 7 to 13). The imagined boast of verse 17, "The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me," is the chapter's pivot, answered at once by verse 18: it is God who gives the power to gain wealth.

outline.t: Remember how God humbled and fed you in the wilderness
The good land, and the call to bless God when full
The danger of pride when wealth increases
Forget God, and you will perish like the nations

doctrines.note: God's care in the wilderness reached to food, water, clothing, and feet. In the land his provision will be less obvious, coming through rain, harvest, and human work, but no less his. Verse 18 says even the ability to produce wealth is God's gift.

The hardships of the wilderness were not random or merely punitive. God used hunger to humble and test Israel and to teach them what they truly live on. Scripture does not say every hardship is explained this way, but it does say God can use hardship to form his people.

Human beings live on every word that comes from God's mouth. God's word is presented as food, as necessary to life as bread. This is one of the Old Testament's strongest statements of dependence on what God has spoken.

words.note: Anah, to humble or afflict. It can describe oppression, as of Israel in Egypt, but here God is the subject and the purpose is formation (verses 2, 3, and 16). The humbling in the wilderness was meant to bring down self-reliance so that Israel could learn trust.

Nasah, to test or prove. God tests Israel "to know what was in your heart" (verse 2), meaning to bring it into the open. The same verb is used when Israel tests God at Massah (6:16), which is forbidden. God's testing aims at his people's good; their testing of him is distrust.

Man, manna. Exodus 16 explains the name with a pun on the question "What is it?" The food was unknown to Israel and to their fathers (verses 3 and 16), which is the point: they could not produce it or explain it, only receive it.

Shakach, to forget. In Deuteronomy forgetting is not a lapse of memory but a moral failure, the loss of a relationship. Israel forgets God not by being unable to recall his name but by living as if he had not acted. The antidote is deliberate remembering.

christ: Jesus lived out this chapter. After his baptism he was led into the wilderness for forty days, where he fasted and was hungry, echoing Israel's forty years. When the devil told him to turn stones into bread, he answered with verse 3: "Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4). Where Israel grumbled when tested, Jesus trusted, and the Gospels present him as the faithful Son who succeeds where the nation failed. In John 6 Jesus also speaks of the manna, saying that it was not Moses who gave the bread from heaven, and calls himself the bread of life. The Letter to the Hebrews takes up the theme of verse 5, describing God's discipline of believers as a mark of sonship (Hebrews 12:5-11).

hard.q: If God knows everything, why did he need to test Israel to know what was in their hearts?
hard.a:
Verse 2 says God tested Israel "in order to know what was in your heart." Readers who confess that God knows all things have understood this in a few complementary ways. Many take it as language adapted to human understanding: God speaks of coming to know in the way a person does, meaning that the testing brought into the open what was already true, for Israel's sake rather than his own. Others note that the Hebrew verb for knowing often means to experience or acknowledge, not simply to gain information, so God is described as seeing their loyalty proved in real life. A few theologians argue that the text indicates God genuinely learns from human choices, a view the wider Christian tradition has generally not accepted.

What the chapter itself stresses is the purpose of the test: not to trap Israel but to humble them and do them good in the end (verse 16). The test revealed Israel to themselves.

questions: Moses warns that the greater danger may come after the hardship, when life is comfortable. In what season of your life have you been most likely to forget God?
Verse 17 imagines someone saying their own strength made them rich. Where do you tend to take credit for what was given to you?
Jesus answered temptation with the words of this chapter. What would it mean for you to live on every word that comes from God, not only on the things that sustain your body?
